---
title: "Exercise: image formation and the PSF"
---

## Goal

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

- describe the **imaging chain** as a forward model and say where blur, sampling and noise enter,
- blur a small object **by hand** with a PSF, and read the contrast of a grating from an **OTF** curve,
- compute the **Rayleigh** and **Abbe** distances and the **cut-off** $2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda$ for an objective,
- recognise **defocus** and **motion blur** from their PSF and OTF, and explain reversed contrast and vanishing stripes,
- *(math)* derive the cut-off from the pupil, and the OTF of motion blur.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked *(math)* are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

## Background

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Forward model | image = sample(object ∗ PSF) + noise: what the instrument does to the truth |
| PSF $h$ | the image of a point; normalised to sum 1 |
| OTF $H$ | Fourier transform of the PSF; contrast kept at each frequency; $H(0) = 1$ |
| MTF | $\lvert H\rvert$, the magnitude of the OTF |
| NA | numerical aperture, $n\sin\alpha$ (half-angle $\alpha$ of the light cone, refractive index $n$) |
| Cut-off | $2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda$: the OTF is zero beyond it |
| Rayleigh distance | $0.61\lambda/\mathrm{NA}$, the radius of the first dark ring of the Airy pattern |
| Abbe distance | $\lambda/2\mathrm{NA}$, the finest grating period that passes |
| Gaussian approximation | $\sigma = 0.21\lambda/\mathrm{NA}$ |

## By hand

**B1.** A row of pixels $(0, 0, 3, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0)$ is blurred with the PSF $(1, 2, 1)/4$ (outside the row, take 0).
(a) Compute the blurred row.
(b) Check that the total brightness is unchanged. Why must it be?
(c) Can you still see from the blurred row that the object had a single bright point on the left and two neighbouring points on the right?

**B2.** Compute the Rayleigh distance, the Abbe distance and the cut-off frequency (in cycles/µm) for
(a) a water objective, NA 1.2, at λ = 488 nm;
(b) a dry objective, NA 0.75, at λ = 600 nm.

**B3.** Two objectives, NA 1.4 and NA 1.2, image blue light (450 nm). Which of them resolves two points 200 nm apart by the Rayleigh criterion?

**B4.** Use the OTF curve of the lecture (NA 1.4, 520 nm; right panel of the Airy figure).
(a) Read off the contrast kept for gratings of period 1 µm, 400 nm and 250 nm.
(b) What happens to a grating of period 180 nm?

**B5.** A 100 nm fluorescent bead is imaged with an NA 0.3 and an NA 1.4 objective (same wavelength). The two images look alike, but one is much larger. Why do they have the same shape? How much larger is the NA 0.3 image?

**B6.** During an exposure the stage drifted by 0.5 µm along $x$.
(a) What does the PSF look like (ignoring diffraction)?
(b) Which grating periods along $x$ vanish completely?
(c) What happens to a grating with stripes running along $x$ (its frequency is along $y$)?

**B7.** In a defocused image of a striped test chart, the stripes in one region look inverted. A colleague concludes the camera's colour table is wrong. Explain what actually happened.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**B1.** (a) Each pixel becomes $\tfrac14$ left neighbour + $\tfrac12$ itself + $\tfrac14$ right neighbour: $(0,\ 0.75,\ 1.5,\ 0.75,\ 0,\ 0.25,\ 0.75,\ 0.75,\ 0.25)$.
(b) Object total $3 + 1 + 1 = 5$; blurred total $0.75 + 1.5 + 0.75 + 0.25 + 0.75 + 0.75 + 0.25 = 5$. The PSF sums to 1: every point's light is spread over its neighbours, none is lost (no light falls off the ends here).
(c) Yes, here: the left blob is symmetric with peak 1.5, the right one is flat-topped (0.75, 0.75) and wider. With a wider PSF the two right points would merge into a single blob: that is the resolution question of the next unit.

**B2.** (a) Rayleigh $0.61 \cdot 488/1.2 = 248$ nm; Abbe $488/2.4 = 203$ nm; cut-off $2.4/0.488 = 4.92$ cycles/µm.
(b) Rayleigh $0.61 \cdot 600/0.75 = 488$ nm; Abbe $600/1.5 = 400$ nm; cut-off $1.5/0.6 = 2.5$ cycles/µm.

**B3.** NA 1.4: $0.61 \cdot 450/1.4 = 196$ nm < 200 nm: resolved. NA 1.2: $0.61 \cdot 450/1.2 = 229$ nm > 200 nm: not resolved by Rayleigh's criterion.

**B4.** (a) The cut-off is 5.4 cycles/µm. Period 1 µm = 1 cycle/µm: about 0.77. Period 400 nm = 2.5 cycles/µm: about 0.43. Period 250 nm = 4 cycles/µm: about 0.15. (From the formula: 0.765, 0.431, 0.150.)
(b) Period 180 nm = 5.6 cycles/µm, beyond the cut-off: contrast 0. The grating is not in the image at all.

**B5.** A 100 nm bead is much smaller than both PSFs, so in both cases the image of the bead is essentially the PSF itself, an Airy pattern. The Airy pattern of a perfect lens always has the same shape; only its scale $\lambda/\mathrm{NA}$ changes. At NA 0.3 it is $1.4/0.3 = 4.7$ times larger (first dark ring at 1.06 µm instead of 227 nm at 520 nm).

**B6.** (a) A short line of length 0.5 µm along $x$, uniform brightness (constant speed).
(b) The OTF along $x$ is $\mathrm{sinc}(Lk)$ with zeros at $k = 1/L, 2/L, \dots$ = 2, 4, 6, … cycles/µm: periods 500 nm, 250 nm, 167 nm, …. Each of these is averaged over exactly a whole number of periods during the motion.
(c) Nothing: moving along the stripes does not change what each pixel sees. The OTF along $y$ is 1 (apart from the lens's own blur).

**B7.** Not the colour table: defocus. The OTF of a defocused lens becomes negative at some frequencies. A stripe pattern with such a frequency is imaged as $1 + H\cos(\dots)$ with $H < 0$: shifted by half a period, so bright and dark swap. Only the stripes in that frequency band are inverted; coarser stripes keep their sign.
:::

### Math questions

**B8.** *(math)* The pupil of a lens is a disc of radius $\rho_0 = \mathrm{NA}/\lambda$ in frequency space, and the incoherent OTF is the autocorrelation of the pupil, $H(\mathbf k) \propto \int P(\boldsymbol\rho)\,P(\boldsymbol\rho + \mathbf k)\,d\boldsymbol\rho$.
(a) Explain why $H(\mathbf k) = 0$ for $|\mathbf k| > 2\rho_0$.
(b) Compute $H$ for a one-dimensional "pupil" $P(\rho) = 1$ for $|\rho| \le \rho_0$ (a slit), normalised so that $H(0) = 1$. What shape is it?

**B9.** *(math)* Show that a PSF with $h(-\mathbf x) = h(\mathbf x)$ has a real OTF. Give an example of a symmetric PSF whose OTF is negative somewhere.

**B10.** *(math)* Motion blur over a length $L$ along $x$: $h(x) = \tfrac1L$ for $|x| \le L/2$, else 0.
(a) Compute $H(k)$ and its zeros.
(b) The image of the grating $1 + \cos(2\pi k x)$ is $1 + H(k)\cos(2\pi kx)$. For $L = 1$ µm, what is the image of a grating with period 700 nm?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions (math)"}
**B8.** (a) $P(\boldsymbol\rho)P(\boldsymbol\rho + \mathbf k)$ is non-zero only where the disc and its copy shifted by $-\mathbf k$ overlap. Two discs of radius $\rho_0$ whose centres are more than $2\rho_0$ apart do not overlap: $H = 0$ for $|\mathbf k| > 2\rho_0 = 2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda$.
(b) The overlap of two intervals of length $2\rho_0$ shifted by $k$ has length $2\rho_0 - |k|$ for $|k| \le 2\rho_0$. Normalised: $H(k) = 1 - |k|/(2\rho_0)$, a **triangle**, falling linearly from 1 to 0 at the cut-off. (The circular pupil gives the curved version $\tfrac2\pi(\arccos s - s\sqrt{1 - s^2})$, which also starts with a straight fall.)

**B9.** $H(\mathbf k) = \int h(\mathbf x)\,e^{-2\pi i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}d\mathbf x$. Its complex conjugate is $\int h(\mathbf x)\,e^{2\pi i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}d\mathbf x$; substituting $\mathbf x \to -\mathbf x$ and using $h(-\mathbf x) = h(\mathbf x)$ gives $H(\mathbf k)$ back. A number equal to its conjugate is real. Example: the uniform line of B10, $H = \mathrm{sinc}(Lk)$, negative between $1/L$ and $2/L$; or a uniform disc (geometric defocus), whose OTF $2J_1(x)/x$ is negative between its first two zeros.

**B10.** (a) $H(k) = \frac1L\int_{-L/2}^{L/2}e^{-2\pi ikx}dx = \frac{e^{-i\pi Lk} - e^{i\pi Lk}}{-2\pi i L k} = \frac{\sin(\pi Lk)}{\pi Lk}$, zero at $k = m/L$, $m = \pm1, \pm2, \dots$
(b) Period 700 nm: $k = 1.43$ cycles/µm, $\pi L k = 4.49$, $H = \sin(4.49)/4.49 = -0.217$. The image is $1 - 0.217\cos(2\pi kx)$: the grating with 22 % of its contrast, **inverted**.
:::

## Explore {#explore}

The demo computes the PSF of an ideal lens from its pupil on a 256 × 256 grid of 40 nm pixels (a 10 µm field), and blurs a test object with it. Panels: the PSF (2.6 µm wide; tick "log scale" to see the rings), the OTF as an image up to ±8 cycles/µm with the cut-off circle $2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda$ in red (tick "signed" to see negative values in blue), the object and its image. The plot shows the OTF along the horizontal frequency axis with the curve of an ideal in-focus lens (dashed). The PSF menu adds defocus, motion blur, or the Gaussian approximation. The micrograph is treated as the true object with 40 nm pixels (it is itself already a blurred image).

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="psfotf" data-preset="oil"></div>
<script src="../demos/dist/psfotf.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Preset **oil objective, NA 1.4**. Write down the Rayleigh distance, the Abbe distance, the cut-off and the PSF FWHM. Check the FWHM against $0.51\lambda/\mathrm{NA}$. Where does the blue curve reach zero?

**E2.** Lower the NA to 0.3 (preset **dry objective**). By what factor do the FWHM and the cut-off change? Compare with the ratio of the NAs. What happens to the micrograph?

**E3.** Choose the **Siemens star** as object. Its 16 bright spokes have period $2\pi r/16$ at radius $r$. At NA 1.4 and at NA 0.3, estimate the radius of the grey disc in the middle where the spokes disappear, and predict it from the Abbe distance.

**E4.** Preset **blue vs red** (NA 0.8, bar groups with periods 160–800 nm, finest top left). Which groups show bars at 450 nm? Move λ to 650 nm: which groups disappear? Use the Abbe distance to explain.

**E5.** Preset **defocus: contrast reversal** (NA 0.7, 2 µm out of focus). In which frequency range is the OTF negative? Find a spoke of the star that changes from bright to dark along its length. Then set the defocus to 0: does any part of the OTF stay negative?

**E6.** Preset **motion blur** (1 µm along $x$). Where are the zeros of the OTF, and how negative does it get? Change the motion length to 0.5 µm and the angle to 90°: where are the zeros now, and which spokes of the star are affected?

**E7.** Preset **Gaussian approximation**. Compare its FWHM with the Airy PSF's (switch the PSF menu to "lens"). Where do the two OTF curves differ most? What does the Gaussian OTF do beyond the cut-off?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**E1.** Rayleigh 227 nm, Abbe 186 nm, cut-off 5.38 cycles/µm, PSF FWHM 192 nm. $0.51 \cdot 520/1.4 = 191$ nm: they agree (the demo measures on 40 nm pixels). The blue curve follows the dashed ideal curve and reaches zero at the red line, 5.38 cycles/µm.

**E2.** At NA 0.3: FWHM 891 nm and cut-off 1.15 cycles/µm. The FWHM grows by $891/192 = 4.6$ and the cut-off falls by $5.38/1.15 = 4.7$, both the ratio of the NAs, $1.4/0.3 = 4.7$. The micrograph keeps only its coarse structure (the nucleus outline); the fine granules are gone, and the red circle in the OTF panel has shrunk to a small disc.

**E3.** The spokes vanish where their period $2\pi r/16$ drops below the Abbe distance: $r = 16 \cdot \lambda/(2\mathrm{NA})/(2\pi)$. NA 1.4: $16 \cdot 186/(2\pi) = 0.47$ µm, about 12 pixels; NA 0.3: $16 \cdot 867/(2\pi) = 2.2$ µm, about 55 pixels, a quarter of the field. Inside that radius the star is uniformly grey.

**E4.** At 450 nm (Abbe $450/1.6 = 281$ nm) the groups with periods 320 nm (faint, tick "stretch") and 400 nm and above show bars; 160–240 nm are grey. At 650 nm (Abbe $650/1.6 = 406$ nm) the 320 nm and 400 nm groups disappear too; 480 nm is still faintly visible. Their frequency is now beyond the cut-off. The readout's cut-off moves from 3.56 to 2.46 cycles/µm.

**E5.** The OTF is negative from about 0.55 to 2.3 cycles/µm (most negative about −0.06 near 0.7 cycles/µm), then slightly positive until the cut-off 2.69 cycles/µm. On the star these frequencies lie between radii of about 1.1 and 4.6 µm: a spoke that is bright near the rim becomes dark in that band. With defocus 0 the OTF is positive everywhere up to the cut-off: the in-focus lens never reverses contrast.

**E6.** Zeros at 1 and 2 cycles/µm (every $1/L$); the curve dips to about −0.14 near 1.4 cycles/µm. With 0.5 µm the zeros move to 2 and 4 cycles/µm (fewer within the cut-off). At 90° the motion is vertical: the stripes in the OTF image turn by 90°, the curve along the horizontal axis is the lens's own OTF again, and now the horizontal spokes of the star (whose stripes vary along $y$) lose contrast instead of the vertical ones.

**E7.** FWHM 186 nm for the Gaussian, 192 nm for the lens. The OTF curves differ most at low frequencies (at 1 cycle/µm: 0.89 for the Gaussian against 0.77) and near the cut-off; around 3–4 cycles/µm they nearly agree. Beyond the cut-off the Gaussian OTF is small but not zero (0.03 at 5.4 cycles/µm): it lets through a little of what a real lens cannot pass. In log scale the Gaussian PSF has no rings.
:::

## Where this leads

The OTF says which frequencies the optics deliver. The next unit asks the practical questions that follow: when are two points **resolved**, how large may a **pixel** be (Nyquist for a microscope), why is the PSF **longer along the optical axis**, and how do we **measure** a PSF with beads.
